ethnic-genetic-fatalism-genetics-is-ever.text: Blackpill and looksmaxxing forum posters use this framing to argue that facial structure, height and ethnicity set romantic outcomes, and it is the stance many self-improvement discussions react against. Attractiveness effects are studied; how fixed they are remains debated.

chain: No grooming, fitness or social effort
ldar-lay-down-and-rot.text: Incel and blackpill forum users use LDAR as slang for resigning from dating and self-improvement, and looksmaxxing communities often cite it as the outcome they want to avoid. The term itself is unstudied, though hopelessness in these communities is documented.

chain: Shapes what people try for looks
cope-copium.text: Forum users apply cope to sort looksmaxxing methods into those they consider real and those they consider wishful, and blackpill users also apply it to self-improvement itself. It is slang for argument, not a technique, so it has no studied appearance effect.

incel-ideology.text: Incel ideology is the worldview behind much looksmaxxing forum culture, centred on the blackpill claim that facial structure and height largely fix romantic outcomes. The community and its mental-health burdens are heavily studied; the appearance claims are disputed in research.

chain: Height seen as a master variable
Interest in height gain and lifts
heightpill-short-king-discourse.text: Looksmaxxing and dating forums use the heightpill to argue height strongly shapes romantic outcomes, which motivates interest in lifts, posture and height-gain methods, while short-king discourse pushes back. Research finds height correlations with dating outcomes; their size and cause are debated.

chain: Guides which traits people try to change
wristcel-ringcel-heightcel-ricecel.text: Forum users apply these labels to themselves to name the single trait (wrist size, finger ratio, height or ancestry) they feel holds back their dating prospects. They are slang self-descriptions, not measurements, and have no studied appearance effect.

chain: Rate faces on a tier scale
subhuman-ltn-htn-chad-tiers.text: Looksmaxxing and incel communities use these tiers, descended from the PSL scale, to rank men's attractiveness and to set goals for improvement. The labels are informal community ratings rather than validated measures.

chain: Feel the goal as already achieved
manifestation-law-of-attraction-for-look.text: Practitioners combine visualisation and affirmations in the belief that thoughts draw matching outcomes, applying it to a changed face, body or skin. No studies test manifestation for physical appearance change.

affirmations-self-talk.text: Users repeat positive statements to counter negative face or body image and build confidence. Value-based self-affirmation has some research, while affirmations for looks have not been tested.

meditation-mindfulness.text: Appearance and self-improvement communities discuss meditation as a way to reduce stress and improve self-image, which they link to a calmer presence. Stress effects are widely studied; effects on appearance specifically are not.

therapy-counselling.text: Therapy is raised in these communities as support for self-esteem and body image alongside appearance work. It is mainstream psychological care, and trials on appearance-specific outcomes are scarce.

journaling-gratitude.text: Users keep gratitude lists and journals as a reflective habit to support mood and self-image during self-improvement. Small studies suggest modest well-being effects; none address appearance.

stoicism.text: Self-improvement communities use Stoic ideas as a framework for discipline and for accepting what cannot be changed in one's looks. Stoicism is an established philosophy, and no studies test it for appearance.

social-media-detox.text: Users take breaks from social platforms to reduce comparison with idealised faces and bodies. Trials show small, mixed effects on well-being, and appearance outcomes are not directly studied.

unfollowing-comparison-accounts.text: People prune their feeds of accounts that provoke appearance comparison, aiming for a healthier self-image. Experiments link idealised imagery to body dissatisfaction; unfollowing itself is untested.

gym-for-confidence-gymmaxxing.text: Gymmaxxing is gym training pursued for a better physique and, as proponents describe it, more confidence. Training effects on muscle are well established; exercise has some mood evidence, while confidence claims are thinly tested.

cold-exposure-for-mood.text: Cold showers and plunges are used in looksmaxxing circles as a discipline habit and mood booster that supports consistent routines. Evidence for mood is small and low quality, and none addresses appearance.

chain: Cut phones, porn and junk food
dopamine-detox.text: Ascension circles use temporary abstinence from stimulating activities to regain motivation for gym, grooming and study routines. The neurochemical reset claim is unsupported by research, and no appearance outcomes are tested.

self-improvement-glow-up-content.text: Transformation videos and posts show before-and-after changes in clothing, haircuts, skin, fitness or procedures, and viewers use them as templates and motivation. The genre is popular, and sources are too thin to assess its effects.

glow-up.text: Glow up is looksmaxxing slang for a marked improvement in appearance, from small grooming and skincare changes to cosmetic procedures. It is documented mostly through testimonials and before-and-after photos.

chain: Better outer game: fitness, style, grooming
social-skills-game-pickup.text: Pickup communities teach inner game (confidence) and outer game (fitness, fashion, grooming) to attract partners. Some principles have academic support, the community draws strong criticism, and effectiveness claims are untested.

charisma-training.text: Users practise the posture, gesture and vocal behaviours associated with charisma to come across as more compelling. Research suggests some of these behaviours can be taught; few sources connect it to looksmaxxing specifically.

exposure-therapy-for-social-anxiety.text: People use graded exposure to reduce social anxiety so appearance work translates into confident interaction. It is a core CBT technique for social anxiety disorder with a sizeable trial literature; appearance outcomes are not its target.

approach-anxiety-challenges.text: Dating-advice and some looksmaxxing communities use self-set challenges of starting conversations with strangers to build social confidence alongside appearance work. The practice is unstudied, though it resembles graded exposure.

eye-contact-practice.text: Users practise holding eye contact to appear more confident and present in conversation. Eye contact is well described as nonverbal communication, while training it has not been studied.

self-compassion-practice.text: Self-compassion is discussed in body-image contexts as an alternative to harsh self-criticism during appearance work. It is linked to better well-being, with little appearance-specific trial evidence.

body-neutrality-body-positivity.text: Body positivity and body neutrality are stances people adopt to ease appearance anxiety, either by valuing all bodies or by making looks matter less. Early experimental research looks at social media content, not at physical change.

chain: Eat by hunger and fullness cues
intuitive-eating.text: Intuitive eating is used as an alternative to diet rules, aiming for a healthier relationship with food and body. It has good psychological correlates; evidence on weight change is weaker.

eating-disorder-recovery.text: Recovery is discussed in looksmaxxing and diet communities as a return to regular eating and quitting restrictive habits. Researchers note there is no single agreed definition, spanning physical, behavioural and psychological change.

muscle-dysmorphia-bigorexia.text: Lifting and looksmaxxing circles discuss bigorexia as the body-image condition in which muscular people feel insufficiently big, often tied to muscle-building pursuits. It is recognised in psychiatry as a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder.
